title: Premature action undermining deductions
full_text:
A superannuation technical expert has noted while super fund members may follow the correct order when lodging a notice of intent (NOI) to claim a personal deductible contribution, there are other timing issues that can undo their intentions.
MLC senior technical service manager Scott Quinn said the process around a personal deductible contribution was understood and that after making a personal super contribution on or before 30 June, a superannuant must lodge the NOI with their fund, wait for an acknowledgement notice and then claim the deduction in their tax return.
“Not everyone will do their NOI straightaway,” Quinn said during an adviser briefing yesterday.
“But there are problems with not doing the notice straightaway where issues can arise.
“These issues with timing around the NOI can be things like if I started a transition-to-retirement (TTR) pension and haven’t submitted my NOI, I lose the opportunity to do so and claim a tax deduction that year.
“It doesn’t have to be a TTR, it could be an account-based pension or juts part of the benefits after the contribution was made. Even a 20 per cent transfer of my benefits to an account-based pension can destroy my ability to lodge an NOI for a contribution received in that year.
“There are other things such as partial rollovers and withdrawals that can cause interference as well, and with a full withdrawal, if you haven’t given your notice, you lose the opportunity.
“You have to be careful around the timing of the NOI. We see situations where the accountant has lodged the tax return before the notice has been provided and an acknowledgement notice received.
“The reason I’m raising these issues is because they are one of the big problem areas when it comes to advice and personal deductible contributions. If we are going to see something go wrong, it’s often with the timing of the notice of intent.”
author: Jason Spits
heading: Superannuation and Investments
